title: Routing & Attributes
blurb: The request has a URL and a verb. Routing decides which action handles it — or returns 404 (no match), 405 (wrong verb), or 500 (ambiguous). Read the candidates and predict the winner.

docs.label: Microsoft Learn — Routing to controller actions

levels.title: L1 · Which action matches?
levels.prompt: Given the request and the two candidate actions, which one does the router select?

failStates.title: That template is one segment short
failStates.explain: "products" matches only /products. The URL has a second segment (42), so the template with the {id} placeholder is the one that matches.

failStates.title: There IS a match
failStates.explain: products/{id} captures 42 into id. You only get a 404 when no template matches the path at all.

levels.title: L2 · Route constraints
levels.prompt: Constraints filter which template can match. Where does this URL go?

failStates.title: "shoes" isn't an int
failStates.explain: The :int constraint rejects "shoes", so that route is skipped entirely. The unconstrained {slug} template then matches.

failStates.title: The slug route still matches
failStates.explain: Only the :int route fails its constraint. {slug} accepts any string, so the request routes to BySlug — not a 404.

levels.title: L3 · Right path, wrong verb
levels.prompt: The path matches a route, but look at the verb.

failStates.title: The path DID match
failStates.explain: A 404 means no route matched the path. Here the path matched but the verb (POST vs GET) didn't — that's a 405, Method Not Allowed.

failStates.title: The verb gate blocks it
failStates.explain: [HttpGet] restricts the action to GET. A POST to the same path is rejected with 405 before the action runs.
